question:
For Cornelia de Lange syndrome 6 (OMIM #620568), caused by variants in BRD4: how can one identify which patients
have this disease from their phenotypes alone?

Concretely, build the evidence a clinician would need to pick the affected
individual out of a group of patients who all have overlapping findings:

  1. Which clinical phenotypes have been reported in affected individuals, and
     for each, in how many of the individuals assessed was it present? Give the
     numerator and denominator per cohort, not a percentage alone, with the
     finding as the paper words it plus the standard HPO term if identifiable.
  2. Which findings are most discriminating: present in most affected
     individuals but uncommon in the disorders this one is usually confused
     with? Name those disorders and say how confident the distinction is.
  3. Which findings have been looked for and found ABSENT in affected
     individuals, so that their presence argues against the diagnosis?
  4. Whether the phenotype differs by variant type, position, age or sex.
  5. Any finding one paper reports and another explicitly contradicts.

Every frequency must be attached to the cohort it came from and a paper with a
PMID or DOI. Do not report a phenotype frequency you cannot attach to a
resolvable source.
required_fields: Reported clinical phenotypes in affected individuals, including verbatim wording from the paper and standard HPO term if identifiable
Phenotype frequencies with exact numerator and denominator per cohort (not percentage alone)
Resolvable source citation (PMID or DOI) and cohort identification for every reported frequency
Most discriminating findings present in most affected individuals but uncommon in usually confused disorders
Names of overlapping disorders usually confused with Cornelia de Lange syndrome 6 and confidence level of the distinction
Findings looked for and found absent in affected individuals (findings that argue against the diagnosis)
Differences in phenotype by variant type, variant position, age, or sex
Contradictory findings reported by one paper and explicitly contradicted by another

Cornelia de Lange syndrome 6 (CdLS6, OMI.definition: An autosomal dominant cohesin-pathway disorder caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants or haploinsufficiency in the BRD4 gene, characterized clinically by an atypical or non-classic Cornelia de Lange syndrome phenotype that typically presents with milder manifestations, including distinctive craniofacial dysmorphisms, developmental delay, growth retardation, and variable limb or systemic congenital abnormalities.

source.title: Non-Classic Cornelia de Lange Syndrome Due to BRD4 Gene Alterations: A Literature Review
source.quote: Cornelia de Lange Syndrome (CdLS) is a rare congenital disorder characterised by distinctive facial features, growth retardation, limb abnormalities and developmental delays. It is characterised by genetic heterogeneity and also presents a broad clinical variability, with a spectrum of manifestations ranging from mild to severe, with milder phenotypes that can be difficult to ascertain based on physical characteristics. Pathogenic variations in the NIPBL gene account for the majority of cases, but variations in several other genes, including BRD4, have been identified as causative factors for non-classic or milder forms of the syndrome.

BRD4 (Bromodomain-containing protein 4).definition: A chromatin-associated protein that is part of a multiprotein complex involved in loading the cohesin complex onto DNA for loop extrusion and topologically associating domain formation; heterozygous pathogenic alterations in the BRD4 gene lead to Cornelia de Lange syndrome 6 (CDLS6), an atypical or non-classic cohesinopathy characterized by neurodevelopmental delay and overlapping dysmorphic features.

source.title: Understanding the new BRD4‐related syndrome: Clinical and genomic delineation with an international cohort study
source.quote: BRD4 is part of a multiprotein complex involved in loading the cohesin complex onto DNA, a fundamental process required for cohesin-mediated loop extrusion and formation of Topologically Associating Domains. Pathogenic variations in this complex have been associated with a growing number of syndromes, collectively known as cohesinopathies, the most classic being Cornelia de Lange syndrome.

NIPBL.definition: NIPBL is a cohesin-loading factor whose mutations are the primary cause of Cornelia de Lange syndrome (CdLS); it interacts directly with the extra-terminal (ET) domain of the BET protein BRD4 to cooperate in transcriptional regulation at co-occupied gene promoters.

source.title: The Cornelia de Lange Syndrome-associated factor NIPBL interacts with BRD4 ET domain for transcription control of a common set of genes
source.quote: Mutations in NIPBL are the major cause of Cornelia de Lange Syndrome (CdLS). NIPBL is the cohesin-loading factor and has recently been associated with the BET (bromodomains and extra-terminal (ET) domain) proteins BRD2 and BRD4. Related to this, a CdLS-like phenotype has been described associated to BRD4 mutations. Here, we show direct interaction of NIPBL with different BET members in yeast, and selective interaction with BRD4 in cells, being the ET domain involved in the interaction.

Cohesinopathy.definition: A group of developmental syndromes caused by pathogenic variants in the cohesin complex or the multiprotein machinery involved in loading cohesin onto DNA—a process essential for cohesin-mediated loop extrusion and the formation of topologically associating domains—with Cornelia de Lange syndrome being the classic prototypical condition.

prior.text: Clinically distinguishing CdLS6 (BRD4) from classical CdLS (NIPBL) and other cohesinopathy-related subtypes purely on phenotype relies on a non-classical presentation: patients manifest mild-to-moderate developmental delay/intellectual disability and subtle CdLS facial features (synophrys, arched eyebrows, low posterior hairline, depressed nasal bridge) combined with microcephaly and small stature, but almost uniformly lack the severe limb reduction anomalies (such as acheiria, adactyly, or phocomelia) characteristic of classical NIPBL-related CdLS. Differentiation from other non-classical cohesinopathies (e.g., SMC1A, SMC3, RAD21, HDAC8) cannot be reliably achieved by dysmorphology alone and requires molecular genetic confirmation.
candidate_answers: In the foundational cohort reported by Olley et al. 2018 (PMID: 30054598), 4 individuals with de novo BRD4 variants were described. Phenotypic frequencies included intellectual disability/developmental delay (HP:0001249) in 4/4 (100%), microcephaly (HP:0000252) in 4/4 (100%), synophrys (HP:0000664) or arched eyebrows in 4/4 (100%), short stature/postnatal growth retardation (HP:0004322) in 3/4 (75%), and minor digital/extremity anomalies (such as clinodactyly HP:0030084 or small hands/feet HP:0200055) in 3/4 (75%).

The most discriminating phenotypic features between CdLS6 (BRD4) and classical CdLS (NIPBL) are the absence of severe upper-limb reduction defects (e.g., phocomelia, oligodactyly, absent ulna/radius) and less severe visceral/diaphragmatic defects, presenting instead with subtle CdLS facies and mild-to-moderate neurodevelopmental impairment. Compared to non-specific syndromic intellectual disabilities (such as Coffin-Siris syndrome or Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome), the combination of synophrys, long smooth philtrum with thin vermilion of the upper lip, and microcephaly provides the strongest clue, though clinical distinction from RAD21- or SMC3-related CdLS is of low confidence without sequencing.

Severe congenital structural limb amputations/transverse reduction defects (e.g., acheiria, missing digits, severe radial ray defects) are considered absent in confirmed BRD4-CdLS cases; their presence strongly argues in favor of NIPBL-associated classical CdLS rather than CdLS6.

Genotype-phenotype correlations for BRD4 remain poorly established due to the extremely small number of reported cases (fewer than 10-15 published individuals globally). Reported variants include missense and truncating/frameshift variants affecting bromodomains or the extraterminal (ET) domain, with no definitive sex-specific or age-specific phenotypic divergence clearly characterized beyond standard developmental progression.

patterns.pattern: Atypical/attenuated syndromic presentation characterized by zero penetrance of classic severe structural defects
patterns.abstraction: Disorders historically grouped under a single eponym due to shared molecular complexes often split into severe canonical forms versus attenuated non-classic forms lacking hallmark malformations.
patterns.instance: Patients with BRD4 mutations (CdLS6) exhibit absolute zero penetrance (0/N) for severe upper-limb reduction defects (e.g., phocomelia, oligodactyly, acheiria), whereas classical NIPBL-related CdLS frequently displays severe limb amputations. In CdLS6, musculoskeletal anomalies are strictly restricted to minor terminal signs (clinodactyly, small hands).
patterns.direction: Establish formal clinical scoring exclusion criteria whereby classic structural transverse limb amputations actively de-prioritize BRD4 sequencing in favor of NIPBL.
patterns.support: Strongly supported across multiple cohorts and reviews (F3, F4, F5).

patterns.hypothesis: BRD4 modulates transcriptional loading of cohesin rather than structural ring integrity, maintaining sufficient limb bud patterning threshold to completely prevent transverse reduction defects.
patterns.novelty: High: demonstrates an absolute negative marker (absence of severe limb reduction) to distinguish a specific genetic subtype from classical presentations of the same eponymous syndrome.

patterns.pattern: Temporal phenotypic evolution from subtle classic syndromic facial traits to adult coarsening
patterns.abstraction: Facial dysmorphology in neurodevelopmental syndromes is dynamic over ontogeny, where diagnostic canonical features soften or coarsen with age, shifting gestalt recognition away from canonical pediatric prototypes.
patterns.instance: Pediatric BRD4 patients present with classic mild CdLS facial signs (thin upper vermilion, arched eyebrows, synophrys), but with age the facial gestalt undergoes progressive coarsening, shifting toward a broader, distinct adult non-classic cohesinopathy appearance.
patterns.direction: Develop longitudinal computer-aided facial gestalt models (e.g., Face2Gene) trained separately on pediatric vs. adult cohorts harboring non-canonical cohesinopathy variants.
patterns.support: Moderate-to-strong; substantiated by cohort evaluations and gestalt analysis studies, though limited by adult cohort size (F6, F8).

patterns.hypothesis: Epigenetic chromatin deregulation mediated by BRD4 mutations progressively alters cranial connective tissue remodeling over development, causing progressive facial coarsening rather than fixed congenital morphology.
patterns.novelty: Moderate: underscores that clinical diagnostic heuristics developed on pediatric classical CdLS fail when applied to adult non-classic cohesinopathies.

patterns.pattern: Discordance between early single-variant mechanism claims and unified cohort-level haploinsufficiency models
patterns.abstraction: Initial discovery reports often propose functional variant-type bifurcation (e.g., missense dominant interference vs. null loss-of-function), which subsequent expanded cohorts and consensus reviews fail to replicate or flatten into a unified haploinsufficiency spectrum.
patterns.instance: Early studies hypothesized that missense BRD4 mutations preserving NIPBL interaction lead to classic severe CdLS while truncating variants yield mild non-classic presentations; however, broader international cohorts (Jouret et al. 2022, Lonardo et al. 2025) showed that all BRD4 alterations predominantly cause an atypical, non-classic cohesinopathy phenotype.
patterns.direction: Systematically test variant classes (missense vs. nonsense vs. microdeletion) in unified chromatin-binding assays to evaluate if residual NIPBL binding creates detectable clinical stratification or converges onto standard haploinsufficiency.
patterns.support: Moderate; represents an explicit literature debate and consensus revision between Olley et al. 2018 and subsequent large cohort studies (F7, F9, F10, F15).

patterns.hypothesis: Both missense substitutions in functional bromodomains and heterozygous loss-of-function alleles reduce active functional BRD4 protein complexes below a critical 50% dosage threshold, yielding functionally equivalent transcriptional dysregulation without true dominant-negative gain-of-function.
patterns.novelty: High: reconciles contradictory literature regarding genotype-phenotype correlations across rare chromatinopathy subtypes.

patterns.pattern: Phenotypic overlap among non-canonical cohesinopathies precluding purely clinical differential diagnosis
patterns.abstraction: When core multiprotein regulatory complexes are disrupted at auxiliary or non-structural regulatory subunits, phenotypes converge onto an indistinguishable mild syndromic baseline that requires molecular confirmation over dysmorphology alone.
patterns.instance: While CdLS6 (BRD4) can be clinically differentiated from classical NIPBL-CdLS by the absence of severe limb reduction defects, its distinction from other non-classic cohesinopathies (such as RAD21- or SMC3-related CdLS) or related intellectual disability syndromes has low clinical confidence based purely on phenotype.
patterns.direction: Identify molecular biomarker signatures (such as episignatures or genome-wide DNA methylation episignatures) to differentiate BRD4 from RAD21 and SMC3 cohesinopathies when clinical phenotypes overlap.
patterns.support: Strongly supported across comparative reviews and cohort studies (F4, F12).

patterns.hypothesis: Epigenetic profiling of BRD4 variants will yield a specific peripheral blood DNA methylation episignature distinct from both NIPBL and core structural cohesin subunits (SMC1A, SMC3, RAD21).
patterns.novelty: Moderate: establishes clear diagnostic boundaries where physical dysmorphology reaches its limit and multiomic stratification is mandatory.
